Slice "internet" (1994 to 2012, with the 2018-2019 retirement of P3P and DNT as the closing record). Scope: the HTTP cookie and its standards track (Netscape 1994, RFC 2109 in 1997, RFC 6265 in 2011); notice-and-consent law and policy in the US (FTC 1998 survey, HIPAA and COPPA, the FTC's 2010 and 2012 reports, the 2012 Consumer Privacy Bill of Rights) and the EU (Directive 95/46/EC, Safe Harbor, the ePrivacy Directive and its 2009 consent amendment, the 2012 GDPR proposal); privacy shocks (FT cookie exposé 1996, McNealy 1999, DoubleClick-Abacus 2000-01, PATRIOT Act, AOL 2006, Facebook Beacon 2007, Netflix Prize 2008); the first machine-readable privacy mechanisms (P3P full and compact policies, IE6 cookie filtering, the 2010 CMU 'Token Attempt' study, the 2012 Google/Facebook P3P bypass; Do Not Track from the 2009 prototype through Firefox 4, the W3C working group, IE10's default and the 2019 end); and the birth of VRM (Cluetrain 1999, Searls's 'Intention Economy' 2006, ProjectVRM 2006, the 2012 book). Extra array 'signals' describes P3P full policies, P3P compact policies and DNT: who speaks, what the signal says, its legal force and its fate. The key contrast for the IEEE 7012 story: in P3P the SITE states its policy and the person only sets preferences; in DNT the PERSON's browser speaks, but only one bit, with no legal force; neither lets the person proffer terms.

events.title: Lou Montulli invents the web cookie at Netscape
events.place: Mosaic Communications Corporation (renamed Netscape Communications), Mountain View, California
events.summary: Around June or July 1994, Netscape engineer Lou Montulli, asked how a shopping server could remember a customer's cart, devised a way for a web server to hand the browser a small piece of state that the browser would send back only to that server. He later wrote that he had opposed the rival idea of a single unique identifier per browser because it could be used to track a user at every website. Netscape's preliminary 'Persistent Client State HTTP Cookies' specification described shopping carts, stored registration details and per-user preferences as the intended uses.
events.significance: The web's first built-in memory mechanism was designed by the site for the site: the person's browser stored whatever the server chose to set, and the person said nothing.

events.title: The EU adopts the Data Protection Directive 95/46/EC
events.place: European Parliament and Council of the European Union, Luxembourg
events.summary: Directive 95/46/EC 'on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data' was signed at Luxembourg on 24 October 1995 and published in the Official Journal L 281 on 23 November 1995. Its Article 7 allowed processing only on listed grounds, the first being that the data subject 'has unambiguously given his consent', and Article 25 allowed transfers to third countries only where they ensured 'an adequate level of protection'. Member States had three years from adoption to transpose it.
events.significance: Made the individual's consent a legal ground for processing across Europe — the legal hook that later cookie banners, and eventually person-proffered terms, would hang on.

events.title: The Financial Times tells readers their browser is tracking them
events.place: Financial Times, Number One Southwark Bridge, London
events.summary: On 12 February 1996 the Financial Times published Tim Jackson's column 'This bug in your PC is a smart cookie', explaining that the leading web browser let companies track which pages an individual looked at, when, for how long and in what order. Jackson criticised Netscape for failing to tell users and noted that the only way to disable the feature was to edit or delete the cookie file by hand. Excerpts were reposted within days to the Cyber-Rights mailing list.
events.significance: One of the earliest mass-media warnings that the web's memory had become an unseen surveillance channel, with no user-facing control.

sources.institution: Cyber-Rights mailing list archive (repost by John Whiting, 16 February 1996, of the Financial Times article)
sources.title: cr> 18Feb96 Tidbits — 'The way the cookie crumbles'
sources.quote: It allows companies to track which Web pages an individual looks at, when, for how long, and in what order.
sources.note: Contemporaneous excerpted repost headed 'Financial Times [London} February 12 1996 Tim Jackson: THIS BUG IN YOUR PC IS A SMART COOKIE'. The FT original (print, 12 February 1996) is not openly online and was not read; this repost is the earliest accessible text.

events.locationNote: The FT's London headquarters at the time (Number One Southwark Bridge).

issues: The summary is supported by the contemporaneous repost: the headline, 12 February 1996, the tracking sentence, 'Netscape's failure to draw their attention', and 'only one way to disable the facility: by manually amending or deleting the COOKIE.TXT file'.

Significance calls it 'The first mass-media warning'. No source on the record establishes that it was first. Kristol (2001) says cookies 'were in use for over two years before they first achieved notoriety'. The fix softens the claim to 'one of the earliest'.

events.title: RFC 2109 tells browsers to refuse third-party cookies by default
events.place: RFC Editor, USC Information Sciences Institute, Marina del Rey, California
events.summary: In February 1997 the IETF published RFC 2109, 'HTTP State Management Mechanism', by David Kristol of Bell Laboratories and Lou Montulli of Netscape, on the standards track. It defined 'unverifiable' transactions — requests, such as for embedded images, whose address the user had no chance to review — and said a browser must enable a cookie session in them only within the domain of the page the user chose, with any override defaulting to 'off'. The two dominant browsers did not adopt that default, and advertising networks built cross-site tracking on third-party cookies. RFC 2965, which replaced RFC 2109 in October 2000, kept the same rule; when RFC 6265 replaced it in turn in April 2011, the IETF called third-party cookies 'particularly worrisome' but left browsers 'wide latitude to experiment' with their own policies.
events.significance: An early standards-body attempt to build a privacy default into the web's plumbing — and an early lesson that a privacy default nobody ships has no force; by 2011 the standard simply described the tracking regime.

events.title: FTC survey: only 2% of data-collecting websites post a comprehensive privacy policy
events.place: Federal Trade Commission, 600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: In June 1998 the US Federal Trade Commission sent Congress 'Privacy Online: A Report to Congress', based on a March 1998 survey of over 1,400 websites. In its random Comprehensive Sample of 674 commercial sites, 92% collected personal information but only 14% posted any disclosure of their information practices, and only 2% of the sites that collected personal information had a comprehensive privacy policy notice. The Commission concluded that industry self-regulation had so far fallen short.
events.significance: The founding document of US 'notice and choice': the answer to surveillance became a policy the site writes and the person is expected to read.

sources.title: Privacy Online: A Report to Congress
sources.quote: Only 2% of the sites that collect personal information in each of these samples have a Privacy Policy Notice.
sources.note: p. 27. Same report, p. 27: 'Only 14% of all sites in the Comprehensive Sample, 14% of all sites in the Health Sample, 13% of all sites in the Retail Sample, and 16% of all sites in the Financial Sample post any disclosure.' Figure 1 gives 92% collecting (base 674 sites, March 1998).

issues: The summary's numbers all check out: over 1,400 sites surveyed in March 1998; a Comprehensive Sample of 674; 92% collecting (Figure 1, base 674); 14% posting any disclosure; 2% of collecting sites having a Privacy Policy Notice; the self-regulation finding.

The title says 'post a privacy policy'. The report reserves 'Privacy Policy Notice' for a comprehensive, one-place description of a site's practices, and a further 14–15% of collecting sites posted some narrower 'Information Practice Statement'. The Executive Summary says 'approximately 2% — provide notice by means of a comprehensive privacy policy'. Without 'comprehensive', the title reads as if 98% posted nothing, which is wrong. The 2% also holds for the random samples only; in the non-random Most Popular Sample, 44% of collecting sites had a Privacy Policy Notice.

events.title: Congress legislates privacy sector by sector: HIPAA and COPPA
events.place: United States Congress, Capitol, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (Public Law 104-191), enacted on 21 August 1996, required the Secretary of Health and Human Services to recommend standards for the privacy of individually identifiable health information within 12 months, and to issue regulations if Congress had not legislated within 36 months. The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, enacted on 21 October 1998, required the FTC to make rules obliging operators of websites directed to children under 13, or knowingly collecting their data, to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting, using or disclosing a child's personal information; the FTC's rule took effect on 21 April 2000.
events.significance: Instead of a general privacy law the US wrote sector-specific rules whose terms — including, for children's data, a parental-consent gate the data holder must pass — were set by Congress and regulators, never by the patient or family.

issues: The summary is accurate. HIPAA s.264(a) sets the 12-month deadline for recommendations and s.264(c)(1) the 36-month trigger for regulations. The COPPA enactment date is 21 October 1998, the rule's effective date is 21 April 2000, and the parental-consent requirement is stated correctly.

events.title: DoubleClick backs off merging web-browsing profiles with names and addresses
events.place: DoubleClick Inc., New York City
events.summary: In June 1999 the ad network DoubleClick agreed to buy Abacus Direct, a direct-marketing firm holding names, addresses and purchasing histories on about 90% of American households, in a deal worth more than one billion dollars that closed that autumn, amid plans to link that offline data to its online browsing profiles. After a public outcry and an FTC investigation begun in February 2000, chief executive Kevin O'Connor said on 2 March 2000 that the plan had been a 'mistake' and that no merger of the databases would happen until government and industry agreed privacy standards. On 22 January 2001 FTC staff closed the inquiry, saying it appeared DoubleClick had not combined Abacus data with clickstream data. On 28 March 2001 a federal judge in New York dismissed a class action over DoubleClick's cookie tracking, holding that the DoubleClick-affiliated websites were parties to users' communications and had given DoubleClick sufficient consent to intercept them.
events.significance: The web's anonymous cookie profile and a person's real-world identity nearly fused; the backlash showed people cared, and the court showed whose consent counted — the website's, not the person's.

events.title: Internet Explorer 6 starts blocking third-party cookies that lack a P3P compact policy
events.place: Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington
events.summary: On 21 March 2001 Microsoft announced that Internet Explorer 6, due later that year with Windows XP, would build privacy controls on the draft W3C Platform for Privacy Preferences. IE6 looked for a P3P 'compact policy' — a short string of tokens a site sends with its cookies — and, depending on it and the user's privacy slider, could deny, downgrade or accept a cookie. Its default 'Medium' setting restricted third-party cookies unless their compact policy marked them as fairly innocuous.
events.significance: By far the largest deployment of P3P (Internet Explorer was the only mainstream browser to act on it) turned a site-authored policy into a gate key. As Microsoft itself noted, the browser had no technical means to check what a site's tokens claimed, so the right tokens got cookies through whether or not they were true.

events.title: W3C makes P3P a Recommendation: websites publish machine-readable privacy policies
events.place: World Wide Web Consortium (hosted at MIT Laboratory for Computer Science), Cambridge, Massachusetts
events.summary: On 16 April 2002 the W3C issued the Platform for Privacy Preferences 1.0 as a Recommendation, edited by Massimo Marchiori with authors including Lorrie Cranor (AT&T). events.place: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, The Claremont Resort, Oakland, California
events.summary: Arvind Narayanan and Vitaly Shmatikov of the University of Texas at Austin showed that the Netflix Prize dataset of movie ratings by 500,000 subscribers, released with names removed, could be de-anonymised: with 8 ratings (two of which could be wrong) and dates within 14 days, 99% of records could be uniquely identified. events.significance: Showed that removing names does not make behavioural data anonymous — so protection has to attach to the person's terms of use, not to the data holder's promise of anonymisation.

events.title: Soghoian and Stamm prototype a 'Do Not Track' browser header
events.place: Indiana University, Bloomington, Indiana
events.summary: In July 2009 privacy researcher Christopher Soghoian, with his research collaborator Sid Stamm, built a prototype Firefox add-on that added two headers to outgoing web requests: 'X-Behavioral-Ad-Opt-Out: 1' and 'X-Do-Not-Track: 1'. It was meant to replace per-company opt-out cookies with one signal sent to every server; Soghoian's own TACO add-on had grown to more than 100 of them. Dan Kaminsky and Mozilla's Mike Shaver had urged the header approach earlier that year. When Soghoian pitched it to industry in mid-July 2009, none of the advertising firms showed any interest, and he never added it to TACO.
events.significance: The seed of the browser's Do Not Track header: the person's browser would send one machine-readable preference to every server, instead of the person collecting an opt-out from each company. But it was only a yes/no request with no legal force, and advertisers were free to ignore it.

events.title: The EU 'cookie law': storing cookies now needs the user's consent
events.place: European Parliament, Strasbourg
events.summary: Directive 2009/136/EC, signed at Strasbourg on 25 November 2009, replaced Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive: storing or accessing information on a user's device became lawful only if the user 'has given his or her consent', after clear and comprehensive information, except where strictly necessary. events.title: Carnegie Mellon finds a third of P3P compact policies are erroneous — many deliberately
events.place: CyLab, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh
events.summary: In a CyLab technical report dated 10 September 2010, Pedro Giovanni Leon, Lorrie Faith Cranor, Aleecia McDonald and Robert McGuire collected P3P compact policies from 33,139 websites and found errors in 11,176 of them, including 134 TRUSTe-certified sites and 21 of the 100 most-visited. Thousands of sites used identical invalid policies that had been circulated as workarounds for Internet Explorer's cookie blocking, and 98% of invalid policies left cookies unblocked under IE's default settings.
events.significance: Documented how a site-authored machine-readable policy fails when nothing enforces its truth: the site 'spoke', the browser believed it, and the person was misled.

events.title: The Commission proposes the GDPR, with a 'right to be forgotten' and explicit consent

myths.claim: Cookies were invented to track people across the web.
myths.correction: Lou Montulli designed the cookie at Netscape in 1994 as a per-site memory (a session identifier, a username, a shopping cart). He says he opposed the idea then circulating, a unique identifier for every browser, because it 'could be used to track a user at every website'. His goal was a mechanism 'that didn't allow for cross site tracking'. Cross-site tracking through third-party cookies was an unforeseen consequence: 'That's the one "gotcha" we had,' he told The New York Times in 2001. He also defended leaving third-party cookies enabled, on the ground that trackers would otherwise use less visible methods.

sources.quote: Third-party cookies were precisely the kind of tracking mechanism Mr. Montulli had tried to prevent through his privacy measures. He describes it today as a surprise -- and something of an embarrassment. ''That's the one 'gotcha' we had,'' he recalls with chagrin.

issues: Misquote: the correction says Montulli 'later called [it] the one gotcha'. The NYT (2001) has: ''That's the one 'gotcha' we had,'' he recalls with chagrin. The correction now quotes it exactly. The NYT source quote is extended to cover it.
Overstated detail: the correction lists 'logins, preferences'. Montulli's post names 'a random session identifier, a username, a shopping cart'. It is now aligned with the source.

Verdict: the inventor's stated design goal was the opposite of the claim. It was a mechanism 'that didn't allow for cross site tracking', and he opposed a per-browser unique ID because it 'could be used to track a user at every website'. The NYT independently says third-party cookies were 'precisely the kind of tracking mechanism Mr. Montulli had tried to prevent'. The claim ('invented to track people across the web') is therefore FALSE rather than MISLEADING.

Checked OK: the 1994 date (the NYT has 'One day in June 1994', and the blog says the meeting was 'around July of 1994'), and his defence of leaving third-party cookies on (blog: the other 'mechanism would not have the same level of visibility and control as cookies').

myths.claim: Do Not Track was a law: once your browser sent the signal, websites had to stop tracking you.
myths.correction: DNT was a voluntary HTTP header, not a law. The W3C never finished it as a standard: in January 2019 the working group concluded its work for lack of deployment. No US law required sites to honour it. When drafting the CCPA regulations, California's attorney general concluded he could not require businesses to comply with DNT requests. In practice recipients decided what the signal meant. When Microsoft turned DNT on by default in Internet Explorer 10, 'others voiced concerns'. In 2015 Microsoft dropped the default, conceding that otherwise websites receiving the signal from its new browsers 'could argue that it doesn't reflect the users' preference, and therefore, choose not to honor it'. The one later legal twist came in Europe. In 2023 a Berlin regional court, in a judgment not final when announced, held that a DNT signal is a valid objection under the GDPR. That was a reading of the GDPR, not a DNT law.

myths.claim: P3P let people set their own privacy terms for the websites they visited.
myths.correction: In the P3P 1.0 standard (W3C Recommendation, 2002) the website wrote the machine-readable policy. The person only configured preferences in their browser, which compared the site's policy with them and could alert the user or block cookies. The person could accept or refuse a site's stated practices but had no way to propose terms. Early drafts had gone further: a 1998 working draft let the user's agent 'Return a Proposal of its own'. As P3P co-author Lorrie Cranor later wrote, 'The negotiation protocol was not included in the final specification.' That is the direction IEEE 7012 reverses, with the person proffering the terms.

signals.name: P3P 1.0 full policy (XML)
signals.body: World Wide Web Consortium (P3P Working Group)
signals.whatItSays: The website's own data practices, in a fixed XML vocabulary: what it collects, for what purposes, for which recipients, how long it keeps data, whether people can access it and how disputes are resolved. A policy reference file tells user agents which policy covers which pages. A site may place that file at the well-known path /w3c/p3p.xml, or point to it with a P3P HTTP header or a link tag. The person's user agent fetches the policy and compares it with preferences the person has set. The person cannot send terms back.
signals.legalForce: None in itself. The specification says P3P 'does not provide a technical mechanism for making sure sites act according to their policies' and is 'complementary to laws and self-regulatory programs that can provide enforcement mechanisms'. No regulator is known to have acted against a deceptive P3P policy (Cranor, 2012; W3C, 2018).
signals.fate: Only limited deployment. Its main use, Internet Explorer's cookie filter, acted on the short compact policies rather than on full XML policies. Fewer than 6% of the 10,000 most-visited sites supported P3P in 2018, when the W3C declared it obsolete.

sources.title: The Platform for Privacy Preferences 1.0 (P3P1.0) Specification — W3C Recommendation 16 April 2002
sources.quote: Although P3P provides a technical mechanism for ensuring that users can be informed about privacy policies before they release personal information, it does not provide a technical mechanism for making sure sites act according to their policies.

sources.title: The Platform for Privacy Preferences 1.0 (P3P1.0) Specification — Obsolete Recommendation
sources.quote: In addition, no enforcement action followed when a site's policy expressed in P3P failed to reflect their actual privacy practices.

sources.title: P3P is dead, long live P3P!
sources.quote: However, to date, no regulators have announced that they are investigating any website for a deceptive P3P policy.

issues: legalForce puts in quotation marks a phrase the spec does not contain: 'no technical mechanism for making sure sites act according to their policies'. The spec reads: 'it does not provide a technical mechanism for making sure sites act according to their policies'. The record's paraphrase 'relies on laws and self-regulatory programmes' also has a verbatim source line: 'P3P is complementary to laws and self-regulatory programs that can provide enforcement mechanisms.'

The fate field says 'Little deployment beyond Internet Explorer's cookie filter'. That is wrong for this record: IE's cookie filter did not use full XML policies. It acted on compact policies, a separate signal with its own record. In the W3C's words, IE used 'the presence of a compact P3P policy as a broad gate'.

whatItSays says the policy is 'published at a well-known location'. The spec puts a policy reference file, not the policy itself, at the well-known path /w3c/p3p.xml, and makes that optional ('MAY'). Sites can instead point to it with a P3P HTTP header or a link tag.

Everything else checks out on the W3C pages. Recommendation 16 April 2002, 'obsoleted 30 August 2018'. 'fewer than 6% of the 10,000 most frequently visited websites support P3P' (2018, BuiltWith). 'no enforcement action followed'. Cranor (2012): 'no regulators have announced that they are investigating any website for a deceptive P3P policy'.

signals.name: P3P compact policy (HTTP 'P3P: CP=' header)
signals.years: 2001–c. 2018 (used by Internet Explorer 6 onward; defined in P3P 1.0)
signals.body: World Wide Web Consortium (part of P3P 1.0); implemented by Microsoft in Internet Explorer
signals.whatItSays: A string of three- and four-letter tokens summarising the site's cookie-related practices (purpose, recipients, retention, data categories), sent in the P3P HTTP response header that sets the cookie. Under Internet Explorer's default 'Medium' setting, a third-party cookie was blocked if it came with no compact policy or an unsatisfactory one. A first-party cookie with an unsatisfactory policy was downgraded to a session cookie.
signals.legalForce: None in itself. The browser had 'no technical means' to enforce the claims. A false policy might have been challenged as deceptive: Microsoft said it could ground a lawsuit, and Lorrie Cranor said the FTC or state attorneys general 'could go after' such sites. No regulator is known to have acted. Sites discovered that an invalid or even self-declared non-policy ('This is not a P3P policy!') still got their cookies accepted.
signals.fate: Widely gamed. In 2010, 11,176 of 33,139 sites had erroneous compact policies, and 98% of the invalid ones left cookies unblocked under IE's default setting. Google's and Facebook's non-policies drew wide attention in February 2012. The compact policy was retired with P3P in 2018, when the W3C said no current user agents were known to act on P3P policies.

signals.name: Do Not Track (HTTP 'DNT' request header)
signals.years: 2009–2019 (prototype July 2009; Firefox 4, March 2011; W3C Note January 2019; removed from Safari March 2019)
signals.body: Prototyped by Christopher Soghoian and Sid Stamm (2009). The header field was specified in a Do Not Track submission by Jonathan Mayer, Arvind Narayanan and Sid Stamm. It was shipped by Mozilla and other browser makers, and standardised by the W3C Tracking Protection Working Group (Tracking Preference Expression).
signals.whatItSays: One bit, sent with every request: 'DNT: 1' — 'This user prefers not to be tracked on this request' — or 'DNT: 0' to allow tracking. The W3C draft added a 'Tk' response header for sites to say whether they complied, and an API for site-specific exceptions. It carries no purposes, conditions or terms.
signals.legalForce: None: honouring it was voluntary. Industry pledged in February 2012 to comply (with the White House saying the commitment would be subject to FTC enforcement), but the meaning of the signal — and whether a browser default counted — was left to the recipients.
signals.fate: Never became a W3C Recommendation; the working group closed in January 2019 citing insufficient deployment, Microsoft stopped enabling it by default in 2015, and Apple removed it from Safari 12.1 in March 2019 as a potential fingerprinting variable.

Soghoian's own history says Stamm 'helped me to put together a prototype Firefox add-on' in July 2009, and credits earlier header suggestions (Mozilla's Mike Shaver, March 2009; a conversation with Dan Kaminsky). The W3C Note says: 'The DNT header field is based on the original Do Not Track submission by Jonathan Mayer (Stanford), Arvind Narayanan (Stanford), and Sid Stamm (Mozilla).'

Everything else checks out. The DNT value definitions ('1 This user prefers not to be tracked on this request.' / '0 This user prefers to allow tracking on this request.') and the Tk response header are in the W3C Note of 17 January 2019. The Note's status says there had 'not been sufficient deployment of these extensions' and 'The working group has therefore decided to conclude its work', which supports 'closed in January 2019 citing insufficient deployment'. Safari 12.1 was 'Released March 25, 2019' with DNT removed 'to prevent potential use as a fingerprinting variable'.

Minor, no change: 'One bit' simplifies the grammar, which is DNT-field-value = ( "0" / "1" ) *DNT-extension. The Note leaves room for extensions but defines none: 'Servers that do not implement DNT extensions SHOULD ignore anything beyond the first character'.
